job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — High-volume threshold.** Recovery is prohibited only when it exceeds 10,000 metric tons per year. A company could recover 10,000 tons annually without triggering the definition.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Per-vessel calculation.** Because the threshold applies “by a single vessel,” an operator could divide production among multiple vessels, each remaining below 10,001 tons, even if the combined operation is much larger.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — Undefined annual period.** “Per year” does not specify calendar year, fiscal year, or a rolling 12-month period. Operators could dispute how recovery spanning two reporting periods should be counted.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — No method for measuring tonnage.** The bill does not say whether tonnage is measured wet or dry, before or after processing, or when material is lifted, transferred, or landed. Those differences could determine whether an operation crosses the threshold.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — Vessel attribution is unclear.** Material may be collected by one machine, lifted by another vessel, and transferred to a third. The bill does not explain which vessel “recover[s]” the material, allowing companies to structure operations to avoid attribution.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — Depth cutoff.** Mining at exactly 200 meters, or in seabed areas shallower than that, is outside the definition even if it presents similar environmental risks.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Recovery” is undefined.** Companies could argue that excavation, loosening deposits, test mining, pumping material, stockpiling, or operating collection equipment is not “recovery,” particularly if minerals have not yet been brought aboard or sold.

8. **Section 2(1)(A) — Covered minerals are unclear.** “Other mineral resources” is not defined and could invite disputes over whether particular ores, crusts, sediments, brines, or mineral-bearing materials are included.

9. **Section 2(1)(B) — Unidentified Secretary.** The act repeatedly refers to “the Secretary” without identifying a department. Because section 6 separately names the Secretary of State, it is especially unclear who makes the ecosystem-risk determination.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — Discretionary risk determination.** An activity outside subparagraph (A) is covered only if the Secretary affirmatively determines that it poses comparable risks. Until such a determination is made, potentially harmful activities may remain lawful.

11. **Section 2(1)(B) — No standards or procedure.** “Risks … comparable” is undefined, and the bill supplies no factors, evidentiary standard, deadlines, rulemaking procedure, or process for revising determinations. That invites inconsistent decisions and administrative-law challenges.

12. **Section 2(2) — Incomplete definition of U.S. person.** The definition omits permanent residents and does not clearly include partnerships, trusts, associations, limited liability companies, or other noncorporate entities.

13. **Section 2(2) — Corporate-law gaps.** It covers only corporations organized under the laws of a “State,” potentially excluding entities organized under District of Columbia, territorial, tribal, or federal law, depending on how “State” is construed.

14. **Section 2(2) — Foreign affiliates and control.** A U.S. company could potentially conduct mining through a separately incorporated foreign subsidiary. The bill has no ownership, control, beneficial-ownership, financing, or anti-evasion rule attributing the subsidiary’s conduct to its U.S. parent.

15. **Section 2(3) — Vessel-size loophole.** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less are not “covered vessels” and therefore have no registration or reporting duty, even though they may participate in prohibited mining.

16. **Section 2(3) — “Equipped for” is vague and avoidable.** Operators might use modular or temporarily installed equipment, or divide collection, lifting, and processing functions among vessels, so that no individual vessel is clearly “equipped for” recovery.

17. **Section 2(3) — Gross-tonnage standard is unspecified.** “Gross tons” can refer to different measurement systems, and the bill does not identify the applicable convention or calculation method.

18. **Section 3(a) — “Person” is undefined.** The prohibition applies to “any person,” but the act defines only “U.S. person.” This creates uncertainty about which entities are liable, including partnerships, government-owned enterprises, officers, contractors, and vessel operators.

19. **Section 3(a) — “Engage in” is undefined.** It is unclear whether the prohibition reaches financing, insuring, directing, contracting for, processing, transporting, purchasing, or providing technology for mining. Companies that support rather than physically conduct recovery may argue that they do not “engage in” it.

20. **Section 3(a) — Limited extraterritorial reach.** Foreign persons operating entirely outside the United States are not prohibited, even if their minerals, financing, equipment, or vessels have substantial U.S. connections not amounting to conduct “in” the United States.

21. **Section 3(b) — Exploration-license grandfather clause.** Any mining “conducted under” a pre-enactment exploration license is exempt, even though an exploration license may not ordinarily authorize commercial mining. The provision could thus transform or be read to transform an exploration authorization into an indefinite mining exemption.

22. **Section 3(b) — No limitation on qualifying licenses.** The bill does not specify which government or international body must have issued the license, whether it must be valid, or whether it must cover the same operator, area, minerals, and activities.

23. **Section 3(b) — No cap, expiration, or anti-transfer rule.** Grandfathered operations have no production limit or statutory end date, and the text does not address license renewals, amendments, assignments, or transfers after enactment.

24. **Section 3(c) — Broad environmental-assessment exemption.** The exemption contains no tonnage, duration, equipment, sale, or scientific-protocol limits. A company could characterize substantial recovery as environmental assessment or combine assessment with commercial activity.

25. **Section 3(c) — Purpose-based test.** “For the purpose of” depends on subjective or mixed motives, with no requirement for advance approval or independent scientific oversight. That makes the exemption difficult to disprove in enforcement proceedings.

26. **Section 4(a) — “Operator” is undefined.** Ownership, chartering, management, and physical operation may be split among several entities, making it unclear who must register and potentially allowing each participant to deny responsibility.

27. **Section 4(a) — No registration deadline or implementing mechanism.** The bill does not say when, how, or with what information a vessel must be registered, and it expressly grants no rulemaking authority to establish those requirements.

28. **Section 4(a) — Overbroad or uncertain jurisdiction.** Read literally, “each covered vessel” could include foreign vessels and operators with no U.S. nexus. That construction would be difficult to enforce and vulnerable to jurisdictional challenge.

29. **Section 4(b) — Vague reporting obligation.** “Describing the recovery activities” does not require locations, dates, depths, quantities, mineral types, equipment, license information, or environmental effects. Minimal narrative reports could technically comply while revealing little.

30. **Section 4(b) — No reporting calendar or retention requirements.** The text does not establish quarterly due dates, the first reporting period, record-retention duties, or NOAA’s authority to inspect supporting records.

31. **Sections 4 and 5 — Registration and reporting are unenforceable.** Section 5 imposes penalties only for violations of section 3. Failure to register, report, or report accurately therefore carries no express civil or criminal penalty under the act.

32. **Sections 4 and 5 — Reporting does not cover all prohibited operations.** Section 3 can apply to operations using vessels that do not meet the “covered vessel” definition, but section 4 collects information only from covered vessels. The principal monitoring mechanism therefore misses some conduct the bill prohibits.

33. **Section 5(a) — No designated enforcer or process.** The bill does not identify an agency or official authorized to investigate, issue subpoenas, assess penalties, bring civil actions, or promulgate enforcement rules. It also supplies no venue, limitations period, penalty factors, or administrative-review process.

34. **Section 5(a) — Per-day penalty is difficult to apply.** The underlying offense depends on exceeding an annual tonnage threshold, but the bill does not explain when the violation begins or how many “days” are chargeable once the threshold is crossed.

35. **Section 5(a) — Timing conflicts with the effective date.** It purports to penalize violations “on or after the date of enactment,” while section 8 says the act does not take effect until 180 days later. This creates uncertainty over whether conduct during that interval is prohibited or punishable.

36. **Section 5(b) — “Willfully” is unspecified.** Courts may disagree whether prosecutors must prove only intentional conduct, knowledge of the underlying facts, or knowledge that the conduct was unlawful, making criminal cases less predictable.

37. **Section 5 — Limited remedies.** The act does not expressly authorize injunctions, vessel detention or forfeiture, permit revocation, cleanup orders, restoration, disgorgement, or recovery of response costs. Monetary penalties alone may not promptly stop an ongoing operation.

38. **Section 6 — Weak international mandate.** The Secretary of State need only “seek to negotiate” an agreement within 18 months, not conclude one or secure its entry into force. There is no consequence for failure and no continuing deadline after the initial period.

39. **Section 6 — “Equivalent” prohibitions are undefined.** It is unclear whether an agreement must reproduce the bill’s scope, exceptions, jurisdiction, penalties, or duration, allowing a substantially weaker agreement to be described as equivalent.

40. **Section 7(a) — Unspecified National Academies process.** The bill neither directs nor funds the National Academies to prepare a report and sets no deadline, required contents, or standard of evidence. It is therefore unclear how the stated condition for lifting the prohibition would ever be initiated or satisfied.

41. **Section 7(a) — “Serious harm” is undefined.** Congress would have no statutory criteria for deciding what degree, probability, duration, or geographic extent of harm qualifies, creating uncertainty and room for competing interpretations.

42. **Section 7(a) — Ambiguous termination mechanism.** The language says the prohibition remains until Congress “finds by joint resolution,” but does not provide expedited procedures, specify the resolution’s required text, or clearly state the date on which the prohibition terminates.

43. **Section 7 — Internal conflict between conditional duration and sunset.** Subsection (a) suggests the prohibition continues until Congress makes the specified finding, while subsection (b) terminates the entire act after 10 years regardless of whether that finding is ever made. The unconditional sunset therefore overrides the purported science-based duration.

44. **Section 7(b) — Complete sunset eliminates oversight as well as the ban.** After 10 years, the registration and reporting requirements also disappear, leaving no monitoring framework even if environmental uncertainty remains.

45. **Sections 5 and 7(b) — Effect on pending enforcement is unclear.** The bill does not expressly preserve investigations, penalties, or prosecutions for pre-sunset conduct. Although general federal saving rules may apply, the omission invites litigation over accrued or pending cases.
